edges.description: Reduced AGT activity leaves glyoxylate available for conversion to oxalate.
Excess oxalate excretion raises urinary calcium oxalate supersaturation.
Calcium oxalate crystals aggregate into stones and deposit in renal parenchyma.
Recurrent obstruction, infection, and nephrocalcinosis drive CKD; after advanced CKD, oxalate deposits systemically.
edges.target: Progressive Kidney Failure and Systemic Oxalosis

nodes.description: Biallelic AGXT pathogenic variants reduce or abolish hepatic peroxisomal alanine-glyoxylate aminotransferase activity, the reaction that converts glyoxylate to glycine.

evidence.snippet: Primary hyperoxaluria type 1 (PH1) is caused by deficiency of the liver peroxisomal enzyme alanine-glyoxylate aminotransferase (AGT), which catalyzes the conversion of glyoxylate to glycine.

nodes.description: Calcium oxalate crystal aggregation causes recurrent stones in the renal pelvis and urinary tract, while deposition in renal parenchyma produces nephrocalcinosis.

evidence.snippet: Urinary crystals aggregate, leading to nephrolithiasis (i.e., calcium oxalate kidney stones)

nodes.description: Failure to transaminate glyoxylate to glycine diverts glyoxylate into oxalate production. Oxalate is not further metabolized in humans, so the endogenous overproduction raises urinary and, with kidney failure, plasma oxalate burden.

evidence.snippet: When AGT activity is reduced or absent, glyoxylate is converted to oxalate, which cannot be metabolized and must be excreted by the kidneys.

nodes.description: Untreated PH1 can cause progressive kidney-function loss. When renal oxalate clearance fails, plasma oxalate rises and calcium oxalate deposits in extra-renal tissues such as bone, heart, and retina.
nodes.id: Progressive Kidney Failure and Systemic Oxalosis

evidence.snippet: The natural history of untreated PH1 is (1) progressive decline in kidney function due to complications of nephrolithiasis (e.g., urinary obstruction, infection) and nephrocalcinosis
high plasma oxalate concentrations result in other organ and tissue damage from calcium oxalate deposition (i.e., "oxalosis")

nodes.description: High urinary oxalate concentration promotes formation of insoluble calcium oxalate crystals, specializing the nephrolithiasis supersaturation module to PH1.

evidence.snippet: Insoluble calcium oxalate crystals form due to high urinary oxalate concentration.
